lesson.title: Change Control: Giving Every Network Change a Paper Trail
lesson.summary: Change control is the discipline of planning, reviewing, documenting, and being able to reverse changes to network configuration, so that when something breaks, there is a clear record of what changed, when, why, and how to undo it.
lesson.body:
Network logging gives you a record of what happened. Change control gives you a record of why, tying a specific timestamped change in the logs to a specific human decision, complete with a plan for what was intended and a way to undo it if it goes wrong. Without that link, troubleshooting degenerates into guesswork: someone says it was working yesterday, several people may have touched the configuration since then, and there is no reliable way to know what actually changed.

A working change control process generally has a few consistent pieces. A change request describes exactly what will be done and why, ideally including the precise commands or configuration diff, not just a vague description. A second person reviews that request before it goes out, since a second set of eyes catches mistakes the original author is too close to see. The change happens during a scheduled window, often a low-traffic period, so its effects are easier to isolate from unrelated activity. A rollback plan is written down before the change is made, not improvised afterward under pressure, because deciding how to undo something is much easier when you are calm and not also trying to fix a live outage. And after the change, someone verifies the intended result actually happened, closing the loop instead of assuming success.

Consider a concrete example. A network engineer needs to change a routing metric on a core router so that traffic prefers a newly installed WAN link over the old one. Under change control, they first write a change ticket specifying the exact commands to be run and the expected effect. A second engineer reviews the proposed configuration diff and either approves it or flags a concern, for instance noticing the new metric would also unintentionally affect a different route the first engineer had not considered. The change is scheduled for a maintenance window overnight, when traffic is lightest. Before executing it, the engineer writes down the exact rollback command needed to restore the previous metric. The change is applied, and its effect is verified against monitoring and the router's own logs. If, an hour later, a downstream service starts reporting errors, the engineer can immediately check whether the failure's start time lines up with the change's timestamp in the log. If it does, the rollback plan is already written and ready to execute, rather than needing to be invented under pressure. If it does not line up, the change can be ruled out as the cause instead of becoming a scapegoat while the real problem goes unaddressed.

This process exists because unreviewed, undocumented manual changes are a well known and recurring source of outages in real networks, often something as small as a mistyped subnet mask or an ACL edited on the wrong device, precisely the kind of mistake that a second reviewer or a clear rollback plan catches before or after it causes damage. Change control does not prevent every mistake, but it ensures mistakes are quickly identifiable and reversible rather than mysterious.
